Application Areas: Marine bacterial stress response and bioenergetics
Bacterial cell division and biofilm regulation
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Redox Homeostasis via Alternative Oxidase: Utilizing NADH/NAD+ assays and Fenton chemistry principles to demonstrate how Aox activity mitigates nitric oxide stress by limiting hydroxyl radical production and preserving membrane integrity in Vibrio fischeri.

Context-Dependent T6SS Specificity: Employing hydrogel culture media to mimic host viscosity, revealing that the lipoprotein TasL acts as a specificity factor for prey discrimination by facilitating selective cell-cell aggregation and targeted killing of competitors.

Cell Division and Symbiotic Fitness: Characterizing the essential role of the amidase AmiB in cell division and motility, and identifying suppressor genes to elucidate how peptidoglycan processing impacts biofilm formation and successful colonization of the Euprymna scolopes host.

Phylogenomic Distribution of AOX: Conducting sequence-based comparisons and homology modeling across diverse bacterial phyla to trace the evolutionary history and widespread distribution of diiron quinol oxidases, challenging the paradigm of their absence in bacteria.
Summary Description: Anne K. Dunn investigates the physiological and ecological mechanisms governing marine bacterial survival, with a focus on Vibrio fischeri and its symbiotic relationship with the Hawaiian bobtail squid. Her research integrates molecular microbiology, bioenergetics, and microbial ecology to elucidate how bacteria manage oxidative stress through alternative oxidase (AOX) and regulate interbacterial competition via Type VI Secretion Systems (T6SS). By employing transcriptomics, mutagenesis, and host-associated assays, she reveals how specific proteins like TasL and AmiB mediate prey discrimination, cell division, and symbiotic colonization. Her work bridges the gap between cellular stress responses and community-level dynamics, offering insights into microbiome assembly and bacterial fitness in natural environments.
